phish.subject: Urgent: password expires in 2 hours
phish.body: Your account password will expire soon. Click below to keep your current password and avoid lockout.
phish.explain: A generic 'helpdesk' sending from an outside domain, urgency, and an offer to 'keep your current password' are classic harvesting lures. Real IT rarely asks you to confirm a password by email.

phish.subject: Your payslip for October is ready
phish.body: Hi Sam, your October payslip is available in the employee portal. Sign in through the company intranet as usual to view it. No action is needed outside the portal.
phish.explain: It uses the known internal domain, addresses the person by name, and directs them to the normal portal instead of asking for secrets. Still make a habit of navigating to the portal yourself.

phish.subject: Delivery notice
phish.body: Your parcel could not be delivered. Pay the 1.99 redelivery fee at this secure link: hxxp://parcel-track-247[.]info/pay
phish.explain: Unexpected delivery text, a tiny payment, and a newly registered domain are textbook smishing. The small fee encourages fast, unthinking payment and card theft.

phish.subject: Sign in — CloudMail
phish.body: A login page with the right logo, but the address bar reads cl0udmail-verify[.]top and the certificate belongs to an unknown organization.
phish.explain: Brand look-alikes and mismatched certificates are strong signals. Check the exact domain, not just the logo, and never enter credentials on a page reached from a message link.

phish.subject: Re: Q3 invoice — corrected bank details
phish.body: Hi Alex, please use the attached updated invoice for Q3. Our bank changed last week; the new account is in the PDF. Thanks, Dana
phish.explain: A payment-detail change from a known partner is a classic business email compromise pattern. Verify by calling a known contact on a saved number before changing any payment details.

phish.subject: Quick favour
phish.body: I'm in a meeting and need a gift card for a client today. Can you buy one and send me the code? I'll pay you back tomorrow.
phish.explain: Urgency, secrecy, and a request for gift-card codes are strong impersonation signals even in internal chat. Confirm on a voice call or in person.

incidents.title: Alert: Impossible travel + mailbox rule
logs: 02:11  Sign-in success | user=a.morgan | ip=203.0.113.44 | geo=Frankfurt | device=Chrome/Win
02:13  Sign-in success | user=a.morgan | ip=198.51.100.9 | geo=Singapore | device=Chrome/Win
02:14  New inbox rule created | name='filter' | move messages with 'invoice' to Deleted Items
02:14  OAuth grant added | app='MailHelper' | scopes=Mail.Read, Mail.Send

options.label: Ignore — likely a VPN
options.explain: Ignoring a high-confidence account takeover signal risks data theft. VPNs still need verification.

options.label: Revoke sessions, reset password, remove mailbox rule and OAuth grant
options.explain: Correct: contain the account, remove persistence, and force re-authentication with MFA.

options.label: Email the user and wait until morning
options.explain: Waiting gives the attacker hours. Contain first, then communicate through a known channel.

options.label: Delete the mailbox entirely
options.explain: Overly destructive action destroys evidence and business data. Contain and preserve.

incidents.lesson: Account takeover often shows up as a login anomaly followed by mailbox rules or OAuth grants — check both.

incidents.title: Alert: Mass file encryption on FIN share
logs: 09:38  Endpoint alert: shadow copy deletion attempt (vssadmin.exe)
09:40  File audit: 1,284 files renamed with .locked extension on \\fileserver\FIN
09:41  EDR: process winupdate32.exe flagged — known ransomware behavior
09:42  Network: SMB writes from FIN-WS-07 to 14 hosts

options.label: Isolate the host, block SMB spread, and start the IR bridge
options.explain: Correct: rapid isolation and cross-team coordination limit blast radius while preserving evidence.

options.label: Reboot the machine and continue working
options.explain: Rebooting does not remove the cause and may destroy volatile evidence.

options.label: Run a full antivirus scan tomorrow
options.explain: Too slow for an active, spreading incident.

options.label: Restore from the mapped drive backup immediately
options.explain: A mapped backup may also be encrypted. Verify isolation and integrity before restoring.

incidents.lesson: Ransomware response prioritizes containment and evidence preservation before recovery.

incidents.title: Alert: Unusual cloud API activity
logs: 13:55  IAM policy updated: role 'deploy' gains sts:AssumeRole on *
13:58  New access key created for svc-deploy
14:02  GetObject calls on 3 backups (unusual for this service)

options.label: Disable the key, review the role, and check CloudTrail scope
options.explain: Correct: revoke the exposed credential and determine what else the identity touched.

options.label: It is a service account, so no action needed
options.explain: Service accounts are high-value targets and often over-privileged.

options.label: Delete all backups to be safe
options.explain: That destroys recovery options and evidence.

options.label: Wait for the monthly access review
options.explain: Active credential misuse needs immediate action.

incidents.lesson: Cloud incidents are identity incidents — keys, roles, and audit logs are your primary controls.

incidents.title: Alert: Web request anomalies
logs: 18:20  Multiple requests with UNION SELECT patterns -> blocked by WAF

options.label: Confirm WAF blocks, capture requests, and open a dev ticket for parameterization
options.explain: Correct: the WAF bought time; the durable fix is in code, plus checking whether data was accessed.

options.label: Block the IP and close the alert
options.explain: Partial: blocking one IP does not fix the underlying flaw or other sources.

options.label: Ignore because the WAF blocked it
options.explain: WAF rules can be bypassed; the 500 error indicates a real application weakness.

options.label: Shut down the whole website
options.explain: Disproportionate for a blocked scan; scope and severity should guide response.

incidents.lesson: WAF signals are clues, not a cure. Track the root cause to remediation.

ctf.title: Decode the note
ctf.hint: Base64 ends with padding characters and is often used to obfuscate text, not encrypt it.
ctf.explain: Base64 is an encoding, not encryption. Decoding reveals the plain text — never treat it as a secret.

ctf.title: Shift the alphabet
ctf.prompt: Decode this Caesar-shifted message: ZDWFK BRXU ILUVW LQVWLQFW
ctf.hint: Try shifting each letter back by three positions.
ctf.explain: A simple substitution cipher preserves word spacing and letter patterns, making it easy to break.

ctf.title: Read the log
ctf.prompt: Which event is the strongest sign of a compromised account? (A) A failed login from a known device (B) A successful login from a new country two minutes after one in your office (C) A password reset you requested
ctf.hint: Think about physical impossibility, not just failure.
ctf.explain: Impossible travel between logins is a high-confidence signal that an account may be in use by someone else.

ctf.title: Spot the indicator
ctf.prompt: Which of these is an indicator of compromise rather than a safe sign? (A) A signed update from your vendor (B) A new inbox rule forwarding invoices to an external address (C) A scheduled patch reboot
ctf.hint: Attackers like rules that quietly move or copy mail.
ctf.explain: Mail forwarding or deletion rules are a common persistence technique after account takeover.

trivia.q: Which control still works when a password is stolen?
trivia.explain: Passkeys and security keys bind the login to a site and device, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

trivia.q: What does DMARC help a domain owner do?
options: Tell receivers how to handle mail that fails SPF/DKIM
trivia.explain: SPF and DKIM authenticate mail; DMARC publishes the policy for failures and provides reports.

trivia.q: Ransomware that also threatens to publish stolen data is called…
trivia.explain: Double extortion combines encryption with data-theft leverage.

trivia.q: Which is the safest way to verify an urgent payment-change request?
options: Call a saved number for the vendor
Ask the sender to confirm by email
trivia.explain: Use a channel you already trust, not contact details supplied in the suspicious message.
Encoding changes representation so data can travel safely; it provides no secrecy.

trivia.q: What is the goal of defense in depth?
options: Layers that assume other controls can fail
trivia.explain: Layered controls slow attackers and create multiple chances to detect them.

options: A unique long passphrase per account in a manager
trivia.explain: Uniqueness prevents one breach from becoming many; length and a manager make it practical.

trivia.q: An unexpected MFA push at 2am should be…
trivia.explain: Push bombing relies on annoyance; deny and report so defenders can investigate.

trivia.q: What does a WAF primarily protect?
trivia.explain: A web application firewall filters HTTP traffic; it complements secure code rather than replacing it.

trivia.q: Which log signal best suggests account takeover?
options: A failed login from your usual laptop
A successful login from a new country minutes after one at home
A normal password reset you requested
trivia.explain: Impossible travel is a high-confidence behavioral anomaly worth immediate triage.

trivia.q: What is a supply chain attack?
options: Compromising a trusted vendor or dependency to reach many victims
trivia.explain: Trust in a vendor or update channel becomes the delivery mechanism.

trivia.q: In the NIST lifecycle, what happens immediately after containment?
trivia.explain: Contain first, remove the root cause, then recover services and review.

flashcards.back: Indicator of Compromise — evidence such as a malicious hash, domain, IP, or behavior that suggests intrusion.
Collects and correlates logs from many systems for detection, investigation, and compliance.
Endpoint Detection and Response — records endpoint behavior and can isolate a host during an incident.
A public knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques used to map detections.
Never trust by network location alone; verify each request, device, and identity.
Email policy that tells receivers how to handle messages failing SPF/DKIM checks.
A phishing-resistant credential bound to a site and stored on a device or security key.
Give accounts only the access needed, only for as long as needed.
Unauthorized transfer of data out of an organization.
A model of attack stages from reconnaissance through actions on objectives.

scenarios.title: Lost Phone at the Airport
scenarios.subtitle: A fictional scenario · choose your response
scenarios.lesson: Fast containment beats optimism: lock the device, revoke sessions, and rotate credentials before worrying about the hardware.

s1.text: You realize your work phone is gone. It had email, an authenticator app, and saved payment cards. You are boarding in 15 minutes.

choices.label: Wait an hour — it is probably in the seat pocket
choices.feedback: Waiting is risky. Treat a missing device as compromised until proven otherwise.

choices.label: Use Find My Device to lock it, then call IT from a safe phone
choices.feedback: Good. Lock first, then notify the team so sessions can be revoked.

choices.label: Post your number on social media in case someone finds it
choices.feedback: That invites scams and reveals you are travelling. Avoid public broadcast.

s2.text: An hour later, a text arrives from an unknown number: 'Found your phone. Confirm your password and we'll ship it back.'

choices.label: Send the password — you need the phone back
choices.feedback: That is a classic follow-on scam. A finder has no legitimate need for your password.

choices.label: Ignore it and continue remote lock + credential rotation
choices.feedback: Correct. The message is an opportunity to steal credentials, not to return property.

s3.text: IT confirms a login to your email from an unfamiliar location 20 minutes ago. What now?

choices.label: Reset email password and revoke all sessions immediately
choices.feedback: Yes. Email is the reset hub for everything else; contain it first.

choices.label: Only change the phone's lock-screen PIN
choices.feedback: Too narrow — the attacker is already using your cloud accounts.

s4.text: You sent a password. The attacker now tries to sign in to your email.

choices.label: Reset from a clean device, enable passkeys, and report the scam
choices.feedback: Recovery is possible, but the earlier password share made this harder than it needed to be.

choices.label: Assume MFA would have stopped it and do nothing
choices.feedback: MFA helps, but you must still rotate credentials and revoke sessions after a confirmed compromise.

scenarios.title: The Midnight Invoice
scenarios.subtitle: A fictional scenario · choose your response
scenarios.lesson: Payment fraud succeeds through process, not malware. Independent verification and two-person approval break the chain.

i1.text: At 23:40, an email from your CFO says: 'Urgent: pay the attached vendor invoice tonight. New bank details. Keep this quiet — board meeting tomorrow.'

choices.label: Pay quickly to be helpful
choices.feedback: Urgency plus secrecy plus new bank details is the highest-risk combination in business email compromise.

choices.label: Pause payment and call the CFO on a saved number
choices.feedback: Correct. Verification on a known channel is the control that matters.

i2.text: The 'CFO' replies: 'Do not call, I'm in a board meeting. Just process it.'

choices.label: Follow the second instruction
choices.feedback: A scammer will always have a reason to prevent verification. That is the signal.

choices.label: Escalate to finance security using the incident channel
choices.feedback: Good escalation. The pressure to avoid verification confirms the need for it.

i3.text: The real CFO confirms they never sent the request. The domain was one character off.

choices.label: Block the domain, report the message, and check for other similar emails
choices.feedback: Yes. Contain the campaign and look for other recipients before closing the incident.

choices.label: Delete just that one email and move on
choices.feedback: The same actor likely targeted others. Reporting enables organization-wide containment.

i4.text: Payment was sent. Finance notices the anomaly the next morning.

choices.label: Contact the bank immediately and preserve the email evidence
choices.feedback: Fast reporting improves recovery odds; the earlier pause would have avoided the loss entirely.

choices.label: Wait to see if the vendor complains
choices.feedback: Delay reduces the chance of recalling funds and lets the attacker continue.

controls.name: Email filtering
controls.desc: Blocks malicious messages, links, and look-alike domains.

controls.name: MFA / passkeys
controls.desc: Stops password reuse and push-prompt abuse.

controls.name: EDR
controls.desc: Detects suspicious execution and isolates hosts.

controls.name: Segmentation
controls.desc: Limits spread and absorbs traffic floods.

controls.name: DLP & encryption
controls.desc: Detects and limits unauthorized data leaving the network.
